rawRows: UK Rail Digital Landscape — Discovery Audit (Pass 1)
Coverage-first inventory checked 2026-09-09. Discovery register only: it deliberately flags uncertainty instead of claiming absolute completeness.

Pass 1 prioritises breadth: current main sites, separate retail/account portals, compensation/refund services, smart-ticketing, parking, Passenger Assistance, lost-property suppliers, loyalty/rewards, international products, third-party retailers, campaign/legacy estates and industry bodies. A row can represent a meaningful web service even when it shares a parent domain. Where a property could not be confidently validated, it is labelled unclear/low confidence rather than treated as fact. The Gap Check records residual research gaps for Pass 2.

pass2.title: UK Rail Digital Landscape — Current-State Functionality & Passenger-Needs Audit (Pass 2)
pass2.subtitle: As-is public-web baseline checked 2026-09-09. Scope: functionality, content/service architecture, passenger needs, journey coverage, fragmentation, duplication and evidence gaps. This workbook intentionally makes no future GBR recommendations.
rawRows: UK Rail Digital Landscape — Current-State Functionality & Passenger-Needs Audit (Pass 2)

As-is public-web baseline checked 2026-09-09. Scope: functionality, content/service architecture, passenger needs, journey coverage, fragmentation, duplication and evidence gaps. This workbook intentionally makes no future GBR recommendations.

Passengers move among a national information layer (National Rail), operator/retailer transaction layers, and shared/supplier platforms for assistance, compensation, parking, lost property, alerts and upgrades.
National Rail is broadest at network information, not transaction ownership
It supports journey/fare comparison, live information, station/accessibility data and guidance, but ticket checkout, refunds and Delay Repay are handed to retailers/operators.

Journey planning, live information, station content, ticket explanations, accessibility and support appear across national, operator and retailer sites; some repetition is necessary, but account/service boundaries remain fragmented.
Refunds, Delay Repay, complaints and lost property commonly move from a branded operator site to a separate portal or supplier, sometimes with a different account.
Smartcards and PAYG exist across Key/KeyGo, Tap2Go, c2c Smartcard/TfL, GWR Touch, MetroSmart, ScotRail and other schemes rather than one common passenger account.
Differentiation clusters around operator-specific service propositions
Examples include loyalty/rewards, automated compensation, seat choice, crowding information, virtual station tours, specialist accessibility guides, upgrade auctions and onboard services.
Accessibility is both national and distributed

National Rail provides station/accessibility data and Passenger Assistance provides a reusable assistance profile/request service, while TOCs repeat local accessibility, meeting-point and travel-support information.
International rail has its own fragmented acquisition layer
BritRail information, international sales agents, Eurostar and specialist reservation processes create separate paths from domestic National Rail retail.
Public-web research cannot expose all system boundaries
Identity sharing, supplier ownership, authenticated account functions, app-only features, data lineage and live-data coverage require SME validation before strategic decisions.

✓ in the comparison matrix means confirmed from the checked public web estate. — means the capability was not found after checking the current public estate or is explicitly handed off elsewhere; it does not claim that no internal capability exists. ? means evidence was insufficient. Capabilities behind authentication, mobile-app-only functions, supplier ownership, data lineage and uncertain legacy services are explicitly routed to the SME Validation sheet. The audit distinguishes necessary distributed information from genuine duplication/fragmentation and records operator-specific capabilities without treating them as universal passenger requirements.

fragmentedJourneys.Passenger goal: Plan nationally, then buy a ticket
fragmentedJourneys.Sites / services involved: National Rail Journey Planner → train-company / retailer ticket page
fragmentedJourneys.Repeated details / account friction: Journey/fare selection may be passed, but retailer identity/account/payment details are separate
fragmentedJourneys.Terminology changes: From national journey/fare language to retailer-specific checkout/account terms
fragmentedJourneys.Potential point of confusion: Passenger can experience the Buy tickets action as one journey even though ownership and account change at checkout.

fragmentedJourneys.Passenger goal: Understand a Season Ticket, then buy it
fragmentedJourneys.Sites / services involved: National Rail Season Ticket Calculator → chosen retailer
fragmentedJourneys.Repeated details / account friction: Retailer account/payment details required after national comparison
fragmentedJourneys.Terminology changes: National calculator → retailer product/fulfilment language
fragmentedJourneys.Potential point of confusion: Comparison and purchase are split across services.

fragmentedJourneys.Passenger goal: Book a journey and arrange Passenger Assist
fragmentedJourneys.Sites / services involved: TOC/retailer ticket purchase → Passenger Assistance web/app or TOC assistance form
fragmentedJourneys.Repeated details / account friction: Journey and passenger details may be entered again; saved assistance profile can reduce repetition
fragmentedJourneys.Terminology changes: Ticket booking language → assistance/access-needs language
fragmentedJourneys.Responsibility changes: Retailer/operator → Transreport/national assistance service → relevant TOC confirmation
fragmentedJourneys.Potential point of confusion: The support request is operationally related to the journey but often separate from ticket purchase.

fragmentedJourneys.Passenger goal: Plan station access and register accessible parking
fragmentedJourneys.Sites / services involved: National Rail/TOC station page → APCOA or WMT Blue Badge portal
fragmentedJourneys.Repeated details / account friction: Vehicle/Blue Badge/account details entered in parking portal
fragmentedJourneys.Terminology changes: Station accessibility → parking-provider permit terminology
fragmentedJourneys.Potential point of confusion: Accessible station information and accessible parking entitlement sit in different services.

fragmentedJourneys.Passenger goal: Find station parking and pay
fragmentedJourneys.Sites / services involved: National Rail or TOC station page → APCOA Connect / Saba / other parking provider
fragmentedJourneys.Repeated details / account friction: Parking account/payment details separate from rail account
fragmentedJourneys.Terminology changes: Rail station information → parking location/session/payment terminology
fragmentedJourneys.Potential point of confusion: A single park-and-ride journey requires separate commercial account and provider knowledge.

fragmentedJourneys.Passenger goal: Track a regular train and receive alerts on a JourneyCheck operator
fragmentedJourneys.Sites / services involved: TOC website → JourneyCheck operator page → JourneyCheck registration
fragmentedJourneys.Repeated details / account friction: Email/route preferences stored separately from TOC retail account
fragmentedJourneys.Terminology changes: Operator brand → JourneyCheck service terminology
fragmentedJourneys.Potential point of confusion: Passenger may have one account for tickets and another for alerts.

fragmentedJourneys.Passenger goal: Claim Delay Repay after using National Rail information
fragmentedJourneys.Sites / services involved: National Rail compensation guidance → responsible TOC → dedicated Delay Repay portal where used
fragmentedJourneys.Repeated details / account friction: Journey/ticket/account evidence entered in TOC compensation service
fragmentedJourneys.Terminology changes: National scheme language → operator thresholds/account/payment workflow
fragmentedJourneys.Responsibility changes: National guidance → responsible operator → compensation supplier/platform
fragmentedJourneys.Potential point of confusion: Passenger must know which operator caused/owned the delayed journey and may leave both National Rail and the main TOC site.

fragmentedJourneys.Passenger goal: Use GWR Automated Delay Repay
fragmentedJourneys.Sites / services involved: GWR retail account → GWR Delay Repay account
fragmentedJourneys.Repeated details / account friction: Same email must be used; separate Delay Repay account still required
fragmentedJourneys.Terminology changes: GWR account → Delay Repay automated-claim settings
fragmentedJourneys.Responsibility changes: GWR retail service → separate compensation account
fragmentedJourneys.Potential point of confusion: Automation reduces claim effort but does not remove account fragmentation.

fragmentedJourneys.Passenger goal: Use c2c PAYG and resolve a journey/payment issue
fragmentedJourneys.Sites / services involved: c2c site/account → TfL Contactless & Oyster account where relevant
fragmentedJourneys.Repeated details / account friction: Payment card/journey history exists in TfL account rather than c2c retail account
fragmentedJourneys.Terminology changes: c2c ticket/Smartcard language → TfL contactless/Oyster terminology
fragmentedJourneys.Potential point of confusion: Rail journey is branded c2c but fare-account evidence can live with TfL.

fragmentedJourneys.Passenger goal: Use Merseyrail smart ticketing / Tap & Go
fragmentedJourneys.Sites / services involved: Merseyrail website → MetroSmart
fragmentedJourneys.Repeated details / account friction: Separate MetroSmart/Merseytravel account
fragmentedJourneys.Terminology changes: Merseyrail service language → Merseytravel MetroSmart product language
fragmentedJourneys.Potential point of confusion: Brand and organisational ownership change during a core ticketing task.

fragmentedJourneys.Passenger goal: Use a GTR brand end to end
fragmentedJourneys.Sites / services involved: Brand content site → brand-specific ticket subdomain → brand-specific Delay Repay subdomain
fragmentedJourneys.Repeated details / account friction: Ticket and compensation authentication may be separate
fragmentedJourneys.Terminology changes: Consistent passenger brand but different transactional estates
fragmentedJourneys.Responsibility changes: GTR brand site → retail platform → compensation platform
fragmentedJourneys.Potential point of confusion: Visual branding can mask underlying service/account boundaries.

fragmentedJourneys.Passenger goal: Use West Midlands Trains end to end

fragmentedJourneys.Repeated details / account friction: Separate identities/data for retail, assistance, parking and compensation
fragmentedJourneys.Terminology changes: Operator brand → national assistance / supplier parking / compensation terminology
fragmentedJourneys.Potential point of confusion: A regular passenger can interact with several separate systems around one journey.

fragmentedJourneys.Passenger goal: Recover lost property

fragmentedJourneys.Passenger goal: Buy a BritRail pass and reserve specialist travel

fragmentedJourneys.Passenger goal: Request an unused-ticket refund on a TOC with a refund portal

duplicationAudit.Where it appears: National Rail; nearly every TOC; Trainline; independent retailers
duplicationAudit.Why it is repeated: Retailers need a journey-selection mechanism, but the same network timetable/fare task is exposed repeatedly across brands.
duplicationAudit.Passenger effect: Passengers can start the same task in many places with different UI, account and fare merchandising.

duplicationAudit.Where it appears: National Rail; TOCs; JourneyCheck; retailer apps
duplicationAudit.Why it is repeated: Passengers reasonably need live information in the service they are already using; source data is industry-wide but presentation is local.
duplicationAudit.Passenger effect: Multiple presentations can disagree in wording/timing even when based on related feeds.

duplicationAudit.Where it appears: National Rail station pages; TOC station pages; Network Rail managed-station pages
duplicationAudit.Classification: Necessary distributed information with duplicated maintenance risk
duplicationAudit.Why it is repeated: National coverage and operator/station-brand context both have value.
duplicationAudit.Passenger effect: Different ownership/content update cycles can create inconsistent facilities/accessibility descriptions.

duplicationAudit.Where it appears: National Rail; TOCs; Passenger Assistance guidance; Network Rail
duplicationAudit.Why it is repeated: Access information needs to be visible at planning, assistance-booking and operator touchpoints.
duplicationAudit.Passenger effect: Critical information can be repeated with different detail or freshness.

duplicationAudit.Where it appears: National Rail; TOCs; third-party retailers
duplicationAudit.Why it is repeated: Industry ticket rules are shared, but each retailer re-explains Advance/Off-Peak/Anytime/Season/Railcard rules.
duplicationAudit.Passenger effect: Passengers encounter many versions of the same rules and examples.

duplicationAudit.Where it appears: National Rail; Railcard.co.uk; TOCs; retailers
duplicationAudit.Why it is repeated: National discovery, product ownership and point-of-sale discount messaging serve different purposes.
duplicationAudit.Passenger effect: Eligibility/usage information is repeated before passenger reaches the Railcard account/product site.

duplicationAudit.Where it appears: National Rail; every TOC; separate Delay Repay portals
duplicationAudit.Why it is repeated: Scheme is national but liability/claim processing sits with operator.
duplicationAudit.Passenger effect: Passengers read national rules then repeat context in operator-specific claim services.

duplicationAudit.Where it appears: National Rail; TOCs; retailer support sites; dedicated refund portals
duplicationAudit.Why it is repeated: Refund is normally owed by original retailer, so transaction cannot be resolved solely from national guidance.
duplicationAudit.Passenger effect: Passenger must identify seller and may move to a separate portal.

duplicationAudit.Where it appears: National Rail; Passenger Assistance; every TOC accessibility area
duplicationAudit.Why it is repeated: Passengers need national explanation, booking interface and operator-specific contact/station context.
duplicationAudit.Passenger effect: Repeated instructions can obscure which booking channel is canonical.

duplicationAudit.Where it appears: National Rail; TOC station pages; APCOA/Saba/other parking sites
duplicationAudit.Why it is repeated: Rail sites need to expose station access; parking providers own availability/payment/account.
duplicationAudit.Passenger effect: Price/payment/account details may only become clear after leaving the rail estate.

duplicationAudit.Where it appears: National Rail/Days Out Guide; TOCs; retailers
duplicationAudit.Classification: Genuine marketing duplication, often intentionally regional
duplicationAudit.Why it is repeated: Operators compete for leisure demand and promote local destinations.
duplicationAudit.Passenger effect: Similar destinations/offers appear across national and operator content, but with different commercial emphasis.

duplicationAudit.Where it appears: TOC main sites; separate Zendesk/ServiceNow/Salesforce help centres; retailer help centres
duplicationAudit.Why it is repeated: Dedicated support platforms add search/case-management features but split the brand estate.
duplicationAudit.Passenger effect: Passenger can move from content site to a differently structured support portal mid-task.

duplicationAudit.Where it appears: Thameslink; Southern; Great Northern; Gatwick Express branded ticket sites
duplicationAudit.Classification: Brand duplication over shared operating structure
duplicationAudit.Why it is repeated: Distinct passenger brands have separate storefronts while underlying operator is GTR.
duplicationAudit.Passenger effect: Passengers see multiple brands for structurally similar retail capability.

duplicationAudit.Where it appears: London Northwestern Railway and West Midlands Railway buytickets subdomains
duplicationAudit.Classification: Brand duplication over shared operating structure
duplicationAudit.Why it is repeated: Two passenger brands expose near-parallel retail estates.
duplicationAudit.Passenger effect: Capability is repeated under different regional brands.

smeValidation.Validation question / evidence gap: Which TOCs share the same underlying ticket-retail engine and identity service?
smeValidation.Why public web research is insufficient: Public branding/subdomains reveal patterns but do not reliably expose supplier/system architecture.
smeValidation.Evidence / starting point: Pass 1 ticket subdomains and operator account pages

smeValidation.Validation question / evidence gap: Exact shared platform/supplier map across all operator-branded portals
smeValidation.Why public web research is insufficient: Some Tracsis hostnames are explicit; other visually similar portals do not publicly expose supplier ownership.

smeValidation.Validation question / evidence gap: Whether GWR/TPE/Hull/Lumo refund portals share one supplier and identity model
smeValidation.Why public web research is insufficient: Common structure is observable, supplier relationship is not safely inferable.

smeValidation.Validation question / evidence gap: Whether ticket accounts and Delay Repay accounts are technically shared across all four GTR brands
smeValidation.Why public web research is insufficient: Public login pages do not fully expose cross-brand identity/account linking.

smeValidation.Validation question / evidence gap: Relationship between delayrepay.tpexpress.co.uk and delaycompensation.tpexpress.co.uk
smeValidation.Why public web research is insufficient: Both hostnames were publicly discoverable; current redirect/migration boundary is unclear.

smeValidation.Validation question / evidence gap: Extent of ticket-and-assistance integration by operator
smeValidation.Why public web research is insufficient: Websites show links/forms/phone routes but do not prove back-end integration, data transfer or staff workflow.

smeValidation.Validation question / evidence gap: Whether any TOC retail account stores reusable accessibility needs beyond Passenger Assistance
smeValidation.Why public web research is insufficient: Authenticated profile fields are generally not visible publicly.

smeValidation.Validation question / evidence gap: Coverage, latency and source ownership for National Rail live lift data
smeValidation.Why public web research is insufficient: Station pages expose status where available but public pages do not establish full-network data quality/SLAs.
smeValidation.Suggested SME / owner: National Rail station data / accessibility SME

smeValidation.Validation question / evidence gap: Data source, prediction method and current coverage for each operator crowding tool
smeValidation.Why public web research is insufficient: Public UX shows the output, not the underlying model/coverage/comparability.

smeValidation.Validation question / evidence gap: Whether JourneyCheck, TOC apps and National Rail alerts use common feeds and whether alerts are personalised identically
smeValidation.Why public web research is insufficient: Public interfaces do not reveal alert engine architecture or trigger logic.

smeValidation.Validation question / evidence gap: Interoperability and account boundaries among Key, Touch, c2c Smartcard, ScotRail Smartcard, MetroSmart and WMT products
smeValidation.Why public web research is insufficient: Public product pages explain local use but not complete technical interoperability.

smeValidation.Validation question / evidence gap: Exact geographic/product coverage and back-end relationship among TfL PAYG, GWR Touch, KeyGo, Tap2Go, MetroSmart, TfW and EMR trials
smeValidation.Why public web research is insufficient: Coverage changes and public pages describe schemes independently.

smeValidation.Validation question / evidence gap: Station-by-station provider map and whether parking account IDs are portable across rail locations
smeValidation.Why public web research is insufficient: National/TOC pages link different suppliers; exhaustive location-level contracts are not exposed centrally.

smeValidation.Validation question / evidence gap: Exact operator/station routing between MissingX, LostProperty.org and local station/operator processes
smeValidation.Why public web research is insufficient: Supplier sites list clients but physical custody/routing varies by location.

smeValidation.Validation question / evidence gap: Current active membership volumes, eligibility and system linkage for operator rewards
smeValidation.Why public web research is insufficient: Public sites show proposition but not account integration or usage.

smeValidation.Validation question / evidence gap: Underlying systems and degree of overlap among TOC business portals, Evolvi/TRAX and Rail Travel Accounts
smeValidation.Why public web research is insufficient: Public pages show propositions but not platform architecture and commercial boundaries.

smeValidation.Validation question / evidence gap: Capabilities that exist in operator apps but are not exposed on public web
smeValidation.Why public web research is insufficient: Website research can identify advertised app features but cannot reliably audit every authenticated/mobile-only flow.

smeValidation.Validation question / evidence gap: Whether publicly reachable legacy/duplicate domains receive meaningful passenger traffic
smeValidation.Why public web research is insufficient: Reachability does not indicate traffic, indexing, redirects, ownership or retirement plans.

smeValidation.Validation question / evidence gap: Identity/persistence model for favourites, alerts and app/web synchronisation
smeValidation.Why public web research is insufficient: Public help documents feature behaviour but not full identity architecture.

smeValidation.Validation question / evidence gap: Which station, fares, timetable, disruption and accessibility datasets are authoritative versus republished copies
smeValidation.Why public web research is insufficient: Public pages expose outputs, not full data lineage or update responsibilities.
smeValidation.Suggested SME / owner: RDG data / TOC digital / Network Rail SMEs

smeValidation.Validation question / evidence gap: Which independent retailer brands are white-labelled on common engines and which have distinct fulfilment/support
smeValidation.Why public web research is insufficient: Terms reveal some relationships (e.g. Trainline/Train Hugger, TrainSplit/RailUK) but not the whole market.

smeValidation.Validation question / evidence gap: Capabilities marked '—' versus those simply not exposed in public navigation
smeValidation.Why public web research is insufficient: A public-web audit cannot prove internal or app-only capability absence with absolute certainty.
smeValidation.Evidence / starting point: Matrix rows marked — should be validated before strategic decisions.

pass2Summary: UK Rail Digital Landscape — Current-State Functionality & Passenger-Needs Audit (Pass 2)

As-is public-web baseline checked 2026-09-09. Scope: functionality, content/service architecture, passenger needs, journey coverage, fragmentation, duplication and evidence gaps. This workbook intentionally makes no future GBR recommendations.

Passengers move among a national information layer (National Rail), operator/retailer transaction layers, and shared/supplier platforms for assistance, compensation, parking, lost property, alerts and upgrades.
National Rail is broadest at network information, not transaction ownership
It supports journey/fare comparison, live information, station/accessibility data and guidance, but ticket checkout, refunds and Delay Repay are handed to retailers/operators.

Journey planning, live information, station content, ticket explanations, accessibility and support appear across national, operator and retailer sites; some repetition is necessary, but account/service boundaries remain fragmented.
Refunds, Delay Repay, complaints and lost property commonly move from a branded operator site to a separate portal or supplier, sometimes with a different account.
Smartcards and PAYG exist across Key/KeyGo, Tap2Go, c2c Smartcard/TfL, GWR Touch, MetroSmart, ScotRail and other schemes rather than one common passenger account.
Differentiation clusters around operator-specific service propositions
Examples include loyalty/rewards, automated compensation, seat choice, crowding information, virtual station tours, specialist accessibility guides, upgrade auctions and onboard services.
Accessibility is both national and distributed

National Rail provides station/accessibility data and Passenger Assistance provides a reusable assistance profile/request service, while TOCs repeat local accessibility, meeting-point and travel-support information.
International rail has its own fragmented acquisition layer
BritRail information, international sales agents, Eurostar and specialist reservation processes create separate paths from domestic National Rail retail.
Public-web research cannot expose all system boundaries
Identity sharing, supplier ownership, authenticated account functions, app-only features, data lineage and live-data coverage require SME validation before strategic decisions.

✓ in the comparison matrix means confirmed from the checked public web estate. — means the capability was not found after checking the current public estate or is explicitly handed off elsewhere; it does not claim that no internal capability exists. ? means evidence was insufficient. Capabilities behind authentication, mobile-app-only functions, supplier ownership, data lineage and uncertain legacy services are explicitly routed to the SME Validation sheet. The audit distinguishes necessary distributed information from genuine duplication/fragmentation and records operator-specific capabilities without treating them as universal passenger requirements.

passengerNeeds.need: Access live journey information, useful content and onboard services while I am on the train.
Arrange travel for multiple people without buying each journey individually.

Avoid re-entering passenger and payment details for every purchase.
Avoid re-entering the same access requirements every time I request assistance.
Be warned when my regular or booked journey changes.
Buy a ticket for a journey beyond the operator's own network.
Buy and hold a discount entitlement digitally.
Buy my ticket and make accessibility arrangements as one coordinated task.
Buy regular travel for a week, month, year or flexible pattern.
Buy travel for my organisation with business controls or invoicing.
Carry tickets on a reusable smartcard and load products onto it.
Change the booked train time without rebuilding the whole booking.
Check whether a ticket is valid for a particular journey or train.
Choose a specific seat or preference when booking.
Compare different times, routes and fare options before choosing.
Compare prices and identify a lower-cost option.
Complete a rail-ticket purchase online.
Control which service updates and marketing messages I receive.
Create a journey-specific timetable I can save or print.
Decide whether rail is a suitable and appealing option for my trip.
Escalate an unresolved rail complaint independently.
Find a suitable station car park.
Find an item I left on a train or at a station.
Find answers without contacting an agent.
Find relevant leisure reasons and value to travel by rail.
Find the most suitable regular-travel product for my pattern.
Get food and drink without leaving my seat.
Get live help when disruption makes self-service insufficient.
Get online while travelling on the train.
Get online while waiting for or moving through a station.
Judge whether waiting to book could change the fare.
Keep an eye on a journey without repeatedly searching for it.
Keep my discount entitlement current without buying a new product from scratch.
Keep my purchased ticket in the phone wallet I already use.
Know I will have somewhere suitable to sit.
Know exactly where and how to meet assistance at the station.
Know how to continue my journey after the train.
Know what facilities are available on the specific train I will use.
Know what is departing or arriving now.
Know when Advance tickets become available for a future journey.
Know where I can leave my bike securely.
Know where accessible spaces, priority seating or facilities are on the train.
Know whether I can physically use a station and what support/facilities are present.
Know whether a Railcard could reduce my fare and which one applies.
Know whether a lift I depend on is working now.
Know whether a train is likely to be crowded before I choose it.
Know which platform I need and whether it has changed.
Leave my bicycle securely at a station and know I have access to the storage I need.
Make sure my bicycle can travel on a service where reservations are required.
Manage regular parking without paying manually every trip.
Obtain the photocard/identity needed for an eligible rail product without relying on a station visit.
Orient myself inside a complex station.
Participate in feedback or customer panels beyond individual complaints.
Pay for station parking digitally.
Plan around a preferred route or avoid a route I do not want to use.
Plan around future closures, engineering and timetable changes.
Raise an issue that has not been resolved through normal support.
Rebook or move my journey after plans or services change.
Receive additional ticket savings and rewards through a specialist partner relationship.
Receive compensation when my journey is delayed.
Receive ongoing value for booking direct with an operator.
Recover the ticket cost when I no longer travel or the service is cancelled.
Recover value when a promised onboard/seat/class service was not delivered.
Register my vehicle entitlement so accessible parking works at participating stations.
Retrieve my digital tickets after purchase.
See and manage what I have already bought.
See disruption affecting my route now and decide what to do.
See service health spatially rather than reading a list of incidents.
See whether splitting one journey into multiple tickets reduces the price.
Set up automatic or post-parking payment rather than buying each visit manually.
Settle a rail-related notice or payment reference digitally.
Tell the railway what support I need and have the relevant operators arrange it.
Travel without carrying luggage through the rail journey.
Travel without choosing a fare in advance and be charged from taps.
Understand a rail product designed for an overseas visit.
Understand a station visually before travelling through it.
Understand rules for luggage, bikes, pets or children before boarding.
Understand station information using symbols and simpler visual communication.
Understand the calling pattern and progress of a specific train.
Understand the environmental impact of choosing rail.
Understand the layout of the train before boarding.
Understand the whole trip, not just the rail leg.
Understand what I am buying and when the ticket is valid.
Understand what a station offers before I arrive.
Understand what alternative route, replacement transport or ticket acceptance applies during disruption.
Understand where the railway goes before I commit to a trip.
Understand whether I can make my journey, when I can travel and what options are available.
Understand whether tapping rather than buying a conventional ticket works for my journey.
Upgrade to a more comfortable class after buying my original ticket.
Use a ticket on my phone without collecting paper.
Use my digital Railcard while travelling.

duplicationAudit.Where it appears: National Rail; nearly every TOC; Trainline; independent retailers
duplicationAudit.Why it is repeated: Retailers need a journey-selection mechanism, but the same network timetable/fare task is exposed repeatedly across brands.
duplicationAudit.Passenger effect: Passengers can start the same task in many places with different UI, account and fare merchandising.

duplicationAudit.Where it appears: National Rail; TOCs; JourneyCheck; retailer apps
duplicationAudit.Why it is repeated: Passengers reasonably need live information in the service they are already using; source data is industry-wide but presentation is local.
duplicationAudit.Passenger effect: Multiple presentations can disagree in wording/timing even when based on related feeds.

duplicationAudit.Where it appears: National Rail station pages; TOC station pages; Network Rail managed-station pages
duplicationAudit.Classification: Necessary distributed information with duplicated maintenance risk
duplicationAudit.Why it is repeated: National coverage and operator/station-brand context both have value.
duplicationAudit.Passenger effect: Different ownership/content update cycles can create inconsistent facilities/accessibility descriptions.

duplicationAudit.Where it appears: National Rail; TOCs; Passenger Assistance guidance; Network Rail
duplicationAudit.Why it is repeated: Access information needs to be visible at planning, assistance-booking and operator touchpoints.
duplicationAudit.Passenger effect: Critical information can be repeated with different detail or freshness.

duplicationAudit.Where it appears: National Rail; TOCs; third-party retailers
duplicationAudit.Why it is repeated: Industry ticket rules are shared, but each retailer re-explains Advance/Off-Peak/Anytime/Season/Railcard rules.
duplicationAudit.Passenger effect: Passengers encounter many versions of the same rules and examples.

duplicationAudit.Where it appears: National Rail; Railcard.co.uk; TOCs; retailers
duplicationAudit.Why it is repeated: National discovery, product ownership and point-of-sale discount messaging serve different purposes.
duplicationAudit.Passenger effect: Eligibility/usage information is repeated before passenger reaches the Railcard account/product site.

duplicationAudit.Where it appears: National Rail; every TOC; separate Delay Repay portals
duplicationAudit.Why it is repeated: Scheme is national but liability/claim processing sits with operator.
duplicationAudit.Passenger effect: Passengers read national rules then repeat context in operator-specific claim services.

duplicationAudit.Where it appears: National Rail; TOCs; retailer support sites; dedicated refund portals
duplicationAudit.Why it is repeated: Refund is normally owed by original retailer, so transaction cannot be resolved solely from national guidance.
duplicationAudit.Passenger effect: Passenger must identify seller and may move to a separate portal.

duplicationAudit.Where it appears: National Rail; Passenger Assistance; every TOC accessibility area
duplicationAudit.Why it is repeated: Passengers need national explanation, booking interface and operator-specific contact/station context.
duplicationAudit.Passenger effect: Repeated instructions can obscure which booking channel is canonical.

duplicationAudit.Where it appears: National Rail; TOC station pages; APCOA/Saba/other parking sites
duplicationAudit.Why it is repeated: Rail sites need to expose station access; parking providers own availability/payment/account.
duplicationAudit.Passenger effect: Price/payment/account details may only become clear after leaving the rail estate.

duplicationAudit.Where it appears: National Rail/Days Out Guide; TOCs; retailers
duplicationAudit.Classification: Genuine marketing duplication, often intentionally regional
duplicationAudit.Why it is repeated: Operators compete for leisure demand and promote local destinations.
duplicationAudit.Passenger effect: Similar destinations/offers appear across national and operator content, but with different commercial emphasis.

duplicationAudit.Where it appears: TOC main sites; separate Zendesk/ServiceNow/Salesforce help centres; retailer help centres
duplicationAudit.Why it is repeated: Dedicated support platforms add search/case-management features but split the brand estate.
duplicationAudit.Passenger effect: Passenger can move from content site to a differently structured support portal mid-task.

duplicationAudit.Where it appears: Thameslink; Southern; Great Northern; Gatwick Express branded ticket sites
duplicationAudit.Classification: Brand duplication over shared operating structure
duplicationAudit.Why it is repeated: Distinct passenger brands have separate storefronts while underlying operator is GTR.
duplicationAudit.Passenger effect: Passengers see multiple brands for structurally similar retail capability.

duplicationAudit.Where it appears: London Northwestern Railway and West Midlands Railway buytickets subdomains
duplicationAudit.Classification: Brand duplication over shared operating structure
duplicationAudit.Why it is repeated: Two passenger brands expose near-parallel retail estates.
duplicationAudit.Passenger effect: Capability is repeated under different regional brands.
